cards.explanation: The answer is furious. Verse 1 says Sanballat was “…furious and filled with indignation.” He already mocked the rebuilding once (Nehemiah 2:19), and now he hears the wall is really going up. I think his whole day just got ruined.

What Sanballat is really saying is that they'll never finish this wall. He asks, “Can they restore the wall by themselves?” and then, “Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” I think every question is a sneer that says this job is too big for them. It's a whole speech dressed up as a pile of questions.

The answer is True. Tobiah the Ammonite, who was beside Sanballat, is the one who says it. Right after Sanballat's questions, he says, “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” So the fox line is in the text, word for word.

Nehemiah asks God to turn the scorn back on their own heads. His prayer in verse 4 says, “Turn their scorn back upon their own heads…” Nehemiah, who is leading the rebuilding, brings the mockery straight to God. He starts the prayer with “Hear us, O God, for we are despised.” He says it plainly.

The answer is False. He asks for the opposite. Verse 5 says, “Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight…” So he asks God not to let it be blotted out. It's a hard prayer, and it comes straight from Nehemiah.

The answer is builders. That's the reason Nehemiah gives. Verse 5 says, “…for they have provoked the builders.” The people working on the wall are the ones he names, and he brings that straight to God in his prayer.

The answer is up to half its height. Verse 6 says they rebuilt the wall “…until all of it was joined together up to half its height…” That means the whole wall is connected and halfway up. That's real progress after all that mockery. Halfway up is still a long way from done, and I think they know it.

The answer is that the people had a mind to work. That's the reason verse 6 gives: “…for the people had a mind to work.” No hired help or bonus is mentioned. They wanted to do it, and the wall kept rising. I'd take a team like that over any shiny new equipment.

They plot to come and fight against Jerusalem. Verse 8 says all of them “…conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance.” Sanballat and Tobiah are joined by the Arabs, Ammonites and Ashdodites. The mocking has turned into a plan.

The answers are prayed and guard. Verse 9 says, “So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night.” Both are in the same verse. Prayer is part of how they answer the threat, and they also put someone on watch.
The answer is False. The guard isn't a daytime-only job. Verse 9 says they posted a guard against the enemies “…day and night.” That's around the clock. Somebody is always awake.

The people of Judah are saying there's too much rubble to ever finish. In verse 10 they say, “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” The voices of doubt are now coming from the people of Judah, not just the enemies. I think that stings more. Plenty of us have looked at a huge pile of work and said the same thing.

The enemies say they'll strike before the builders know or see a thing. Their plan in verse 11 is, “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” It's meant to be a surprise attack. This part of the story is heavy, and the threat is serious.
The answer is ten. Verse 12 says the Jews who lived nearby “…told us ten times over…” Ten! That's a whole lot of the same message. I think Nehemiah heard it loud and clear.

Nehemiah stations men behind the lowest sections of the wall. Verse 13 says, “So I stationed men behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the vulnerable areas.” Nehemiah puts people where the wall is weakest. That's the spot to guard, and he knew it.

The answer is False. Nothing there separates the men from their families. Verse 13 says, “I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows.” He stations them by families. I think that makes the posts mean a lot more.
The answer is afraid. Nehemiah stands up and says, “Do not be afraid of them.” Then he tells them where to look: “Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome…” Fear gets answered with remembering.

Nehemiah tells them to fight for their families and their homes. His list in verse 14 is, “…fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” He's naming the people and the homes. I think that's a lot to stand up for.
The answer is True. Verse 15 says the enemies heard “…that we were aware of their scheme and that God had frustrated it…” Nehemiah gives God the credit for it. The plan didn't go through.
Each of the builders goes back to his own work on the wall. Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” Back to the wall they go. The scare doesn't send them home.

The answers are work and spears. Verse 16 says, “…half of my servants did the work while the other half held spears, shields, bows, and armor.” One half builds and the other half guards. I think that's a smart way to split a crew.
The answer is False. No swords stay home. Verse 18 says, “And each of the builders worked with his sword strapped at his side.” They build and stay ready.

Nehemiah tells them to rally to wherever the horn sounds. He says, “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there.” The builders are spread out far along the wall, so the horn tells them where to gather. It's a simple signal for a big job.
The answer is True. Verse 20 ends with, “Our God will fight for us!” Nehemiah says it right after telling them about the horn. The people hear it from him.

They keep at it from dawn until the stars come out. Verse 21 says they kept going “…from the break of dawn until the stars came out.” That's a full day of work, and half the men are holding spears the whole time. I'd need a nap just reading it.

The answer is Jerusalem. Verse 22 has Nehemiah say, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem…” They stay in the city. Every man and his servant is included, so nobody is left out of the order.

Nehemiah wants them there to stand guard by night and work by day. That's his reason in verse 22: “…so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” So guard duty takes the night and the building takes the day. I think that's a full schedule for one crew.

The answer is True. Verse 23 says, “…neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes…” Nehemiah is in this with everyone else. That's one long stretch in the same outfit.

They carry their weapons even to go out for water. Verse 23 ends, “each carried his weapon, even to go for water.” Even a simple trip for water comes with a weapon. I think that shows how alert they stay.
